passages.happening:
The men of Ephraim gather, cross the Jordan to Zaphon, and confront Jephthah. “Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down with you inside!” (verse 1).

Jephthah answers that he did call them and they did not come to save him. So he risked his life, and the LORD gave him the victory. “Why then have you come today to fight against me?” (verses 2-3).

He gathers the men of Gilead and fights Ephraim. The Ephraimites had mocked the Gileadites as runaways from Ephraim (verse 4). The men of Gilead seize the fords of the Jordan. Whenever a man fleeing from Ephraim asks to cross, they ask him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he says no, they tell him, “Please say Shibboleth.” If he says Sibboleth, because he cannot say the word correctly, they seize him and kill him at the fords of the Jordan (verses 5-6). That day 42,000 men of Ephraim die.

Jephthah judges Israel six years. When he dies, he is buried in one of the towns of Gilead (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Ephraim was one of the largest tribes, in the central hills west of the Jordan, and it seems to have seen itself as the natural leader of the north. It had made the same complaint to Gideon, who calmed it with a generous word (8:1-3). Jephthah, an outsider who had fought for every bit of his place, gives no soft answer.

The quarrel is about honor. Ephraim is angry at being left out, and it threatens to burn Jephthah's house down with him inside. The Ephraimites also mock the people of Gilead as runaways, a taunt that played on tribal pride and on the river that divided the tribes east of the Jordan from the rest.

The fords were the crossing places of the river, and whoever held them controlled who could pass. The test at the fords relied on a difference of accent. The Hebrew word shibboleth can mean an ear of grain or a flowing stream. Its meaning did not matter. Its sound did. The Ephraimites, it seems, could not say the opening sh, and said s instead. Tribes that shared one language and one covenant had grown into separate communities, and now a single word decided life or death.

The word has passed into English for any password or habit of speech that marks who belongs. That use comes straight from this chapter.

The number killed, 42,000, is one of many large numbers in Judges. Some scholars think the Hebrew word usually translated thousand can also mean a clan unit or a company of soldiers, which would make the number of men much smaller. Others read the figures as they stand. Both views are held by readers who take the account as history.

For the first time in the book, a judge's sword is turned mainly against fellow Israelites. More die at the fords than are said to have died in the war with Ammon. The book is moving toward the civil war of its last chapters.
passages.later:
A proverb describes what happened between these tribes: “An offended brother is harder to win than a fortified city, and disputes are like the bars of a castle” (Proverbs 18:19).

A psalm sings what they had lost: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1). And Paul warns a church of the same danger: “But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15).
passages.hard:
Why does Israel's own judge lead the killing of tens of thousands of fellow Israelites?

The text does not approve the slaughter. It records it. Ephraim was the aggressor and threatened to burn Jephthah's house, and a war of defense might be understood. But the killing at the fords went far beyond defense. Men who were running away were picked out by their accent and put to death.

The narrator places this straight after Jephthah's vow, and the pattern is consistent. Judges shows leaders who begin as deliverers and end by harming their own people: Gideon's revenge on Succoth and Penuel, Abimelech's massacre, and now this. The book does not excuse Jephthah. It shows why Israel needed something better than judges.

As for the number, reading the word for thousand as a military unit would make the scale smaller. It would not make the wrong any less.
passages.asks: Ephraim's quarrel began with wounded pride at being left out. Ask how pride and rivalry turn into real harm between people who should be on the same side, in a family, a town or a church. And ask what shibboleths your own community uses to decide who belongs, and whom they have shut out.

passages.happening:
After Jephthah, Ibzan of Bethlehem judges Israel. He has thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gives his daughters in marriage outside his clan and brings in thirty wives from elsewhere for his sons. He judges Israel seven years, dies and is buried in Bethlehem (verses 8-10).

After him Elon of the tribe of Zebulun judges Israel ten years, and is buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun (verses 11-12).

Then Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, judges Israel. “He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. And he judged Israel eight years” (verse 14). He is buried at Pirathon in Ephraim (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The pace changes completely. After the slaughter at the fords come three short notices in a fixed pattern: a name, a place, a word about family, the years he judged, and where he was buried. The calm of the pattern is striking after what came before. Jephthah's own notice in verse 7 uses the same pattern, placing him in the list of Israel's judges in spite of everything.

Many children, marriages arranged outside the clan, and sons riding donkeys were signs of wealth, standing and alliances. Marrying daughters into other clans and bringing wives in from elsewhere built ties of obligation across the tribes. Jair, in chapter 10, had thirty sons on thirty donkeys too.

Ibzan's Bethlehem may be the well-known town in Judah, or a Bethlehem in the land of Zebulun. Readers differ. Aijalon in Zebulun is otherwise unknown. Pirathon lay in the hill country of Ephraim.

These notices suggest years of quiet. Even in a disordered age, Israel was not left without leaders. And then the quiet ends, and the last and strangest of the judges is born.
passages.later: The book of Joshua lists a Bethlehem among the towns of Zebulun: “It also included Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem” (Joshua 19:15).
passages.asks: Ibzan, Elon and Abdon are remembered for families, marriages and quiet years. Ask how much you value faithful but unremarkable leadership. And ask what ties of trust you are building between your own people and others, ties that could hold when a quarrel comes.
